title: Circumcision, the way of Ibrahim
hook: five habits of the fitrah, and the one traced to Ibrahim

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baby's first hair, and your line: weight in silver. Did something small go out in a child's name? Today, one more custom of early life, and the last day of this week. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

Five small habits, listed together in one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says five things belong to the fitrah, the natural way people are made. In paraphrase: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the mustache, clipping the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. Four of them belong on anyone's bathroom shelf, done again and again. The first one is different. It's done once, not over and over, and tradition traces it back to a single person. Today's word is khitan, and the name behind it is Ibrahim.
screen: `FIVE THINGS OF THE FITRAH.` → `FOUR, DONE AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `ONE, DONE ONCE.`

segments.voice: Khitan means circumcision: for a boy, the removal of the foreskin. The Qur'an doesn't spell it out. The teaching comes through hadith, and through one name. In another report in Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet says that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, circumcised himself, with an adze, and the report says he was eighty years old. An old man, keeping a sign in his own body. Second, why Ibrahim carries so much weight here. The Qur'an tells the Prophet to follow him. In Pickthall's translation: "Follow the religion of Abraham, as one by nature upright." Upright by nature: close to the idea of fitrah from the hook. So Muslims keep khitan as part of the millah of Ibrahim, the way of Ibrahim, carried on by those who follow him. Third, a neighbor. Jews trace circumcision to Abraham too, in the book of Genesis, as a sign of the covenant. Two families of faith, one shared ancestor, and a shared mark. Fourth, the schools. Muslim scholars differ on how binding it is: some schools count it obligatory, others a strongly emphasized sunnah. And families choose different times: some on the seventh day, some later in childhood, some with a celebration. Last, respect. This is a custom of the body and of the family. The way to learn about it is the way anyone would want their own customs learned: listen, ask kindly, and let the people who keep it explain what it means to them.
screen: `KHITAN, TRACED TO IBRAHIM.` · `FOLLOW THE RELIGION OF ABRAHAM.` · `A MARK SHARED WITH A NEIGHBOR.` · `THE SCHOOLS WEIGH IT DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about the custom respectfully. Settle, and breathe. Think of a custom from your own family that marks a child as belonging: a name, a blessing, a ceremony, a first haircut, a photo on the wall. Imagine a stranger making fun of it. Then imagine someone asking about it kindly, and really listening. Hold that second picture. Then think of one question you could ask, kindly, about a custom that isn't yours, and how you'd listen to the answer. The bell holds the time.
Khitan. Circumcision, kept by Muslims as part of the fitrah and the way of Ibrahim. Today's word.
Your line: the way of ibrahim. Today, if a custom you don't share comes up, ask about it with the care you'd want for your own. Tomorrow, teaching prayer. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim families circumcise boys as part of the fitrah and the way of Ibrahim; the timing varies by family and culture, from the first days of life to later childhood, sometimes with a family celebration.

fork.setup: the Prophet names five things of the fitrah. one of them, a report in Bukhari says, goes back to Ibrahim himself. which one?
fork.reveal: circumcision. the report says Ibrahim circumcised himself, in old age, with an adze.

trapdoor: what you thought: a medical procedure.
what it means: one of the five things of the fitrah, kept as part of the way of Ibrahim and often marked by family.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's five of the fitrah and the report of Ibrahim's own circumcision, read with 16:123's 'follow the religion of Abraham'; the schools differ on whether it is obligatory.
